title.en: Science, art and learning in the Gupta age

text.en:
At a village school the master drew a small circle on the slate and said, "This tiny round zero changed the way the whole world does mathematics."
"Who discovered it?" asked a student. "Indian scholars developed the decimal system with zero," said the master.

The Gupta Empire (about 320 to 550 CE) is often called a golden age of creativity. Rulers such as Chandragupta I, Samudragupta and Chandragupta II supported learning and the arts.
Aryabhata was a great mathematician and astronomer. He explained that the Earth rotates on its axis and gave a good value of pi. Indian scholars developed the decimal place-value system and the use of zero. Varahamihira wrote about astronomy and Kalidasa wrote beautiful Sanskrit plays and poems.
Gupta artists made fine sculptures, temples and paintings, such as those at Ajanta. The iron pillar at Delhi has not rusted in more than 1500 years. Nalanda later became a great centre of learning.
The Gupta age was a time of great creativity in science, art and literature.
Aryabhata explained that the Earth turns on its axis. Indian scholars developed the zero and decimal system.
Kalidasa wrote fine plays and poems in Sanskrit.
The iron pillar of Delhi has not rusted in more than fifteen hundred years.

problem.en: Why is the invention of the zero so important?

text.en: Zero lets us show place value, for example ten as one and zero.
It makes calculation with big numbers simple.
The world still uses this system, so zero changed mathematics.

prompt.en: A friend says Indians had no scientists in ancient times. How will you respond?

requiredIdeas.en: Aryabhata and Varahamihira were great scholars in the Gupta age.
India gave the world zero and the decimal system.

points.en: The Gupta age was a golden age of creativity.
Aryabhata, Kalidasa and Varahamihira were famous scholars.
The iron pillar of Delhi shows skilled metalwork.
